html:
The Nobel Prize in Literature is a prize given each year since 1901 by the Swedish Academy to a writer for their whole body of work. It is one of the five prizes set up by the will of Alfred Nobel, the Swedish inventor of dynamite, who asked that it go to the most outstanding work "in an ideal direction".

For its first decades it went almost always to Europeans, and great writers such as Leo Tolstoy were passed over. Its firsts beyond Europe mark how world literature came to be read:

  • 1913: Rabindranath Tagore, the first winner from outside Europe.
  • 1945: Gabriela Mistral, the first from Latin America.
  • 1982: Gabriel García Márquez.
  • 1986: Wole Soyinka, the first African.
  • 1988: Naguib Mahfouz, the first writer in Arabic.
  • 1992: Derek Walcott of St Lucia.
  • 2006: Orhan Pamuk of Turkey.
  • 2024: Han Kang, the first Korean.

It is still criticised for leaning toward European languages, and for some choices made on politics more than writing.
